title: Ukraine’s preschool system turns demographic shock and wartime disruption into a territorial care, labor, and recovery challenge
source_unit: World Bank, Spending Better on Ukraine’s Youngest Learners: A Public Expenditure and Institutional Review of Early Childhood and Preschool Education
geography: Ukraine nationally, with hromada, oblast, and local preschool-system variation

observations.period: 2021-2024; Ukraine early childhood and preschool education enrollment

denominator.unit: Ukraine ECPE enrollment frame covering children ages 0-5 and enrolled children in preschool education institutions

enrollment_change.value: enrollment declined 31.1%, from about 1.1 million children in 2021 to 765,576 in 2024

participation.value: participation among children ages 0-5 remained between 40% and 51%, with particularly low participation among children ages 0-2

territorial_gap.value: hromadas with the highest enrollment serve nearly three times as many children as those with the lowest enrollment

occupancy.value: 81% of preschool places are occupied nationally, while occupancy ranges from about 52% to more than 100% across oblasts

mechanism.value: war-related disruption, displacement, demographic decline, safety conditions, and local demand shifts produce simultaneous overcrowding, unmet demand, and excess capacity

observations.method: Public expenditure, administrative, and household-survey analysis using primarily 2024 data, complemented by policy review and semistructured interviews conducted in late 2025.
observations.uncertainty: The report notes changing security conditions, territorial-coverage differences, measurement uncertainty, and the fact that quantitative analysis largely predates implementation of the Preschool Law on January 1, 2025; the figures do not identify causal effects of any single disruption.
observations.subgroup: Young children, displaced families, caregivers, women with young children, hromadas facing overcrowding, and communities with shrinking child populations or excess preschool capacity.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower enrollment may partly reflect demographic decline, displacement, household choice, safety concerns, and changing data coverage rather than only deteriorating service quality; excess capacity can also create an opportunity for expansion if networks are redesigned.

observations.period: 2024; ECPE financing and territorial equity across Ukrainian hromadas

denominator.unit: Ukraine local-finance comparison frame covering reporting hromadas

per_child_spending.value: per-child ECPE spending varies nearly 50-fold between the highest- and lowest-spending hromadas

enrollment_association.value: children in lower-spending communities are less likely to be enrolled in ECPE

financing_structure.value: ECPE is financed almost entirely through local budgets, so differences in local fiscal capacity continue to translate into disparities in spending and outcomes despite fiscal equalization

policy_window.value: the report estimates that current funding can accommodate current enrollment and could support expansion if networks, staffing, and service delivery become more efficient

mechanism.value: the place where a child lives acts as a proxy for the fiscal capacity and adaptive room of the local care system

observations.method: Subnational expenditure, enrollment, capacity, and fiscal analysis linked to the governance and financing arrangements of hromadas and central government.
observations.uncertainty: The association between spending and enrollment is not a causal estimate; local spending also reflects costs, geography, staffing, safety, demand, and reporting conditions, and the report does not establish that equalizing inputs alone would equalize outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Children and caregivers in fiscally weaker hromadas, local governments, preschool providers, displaced households, and women whose labor-force participation depends on reliable childcare.
observations.counterinterpretation: Local financing can improve responsiveness and accountability; national equalization or output-based formulas may introduce new administrative burdens or fail if local implementation capacity remains weak.

observations.period: 2024-2026; ECPE staffing, budget rules, and implementation of the 2024 Preschool Law

denominator.unit: Ukraine ECPE workforce and institutional frame covering reviewed public preschool education institutions

staffing_mix.value: more than half of ECPE staff are non-pedagogical or technical staff, and less than half of pedagogical staff are classroom teachers

teacher_pay.value: public-sector teacher pay is 22% lower than private-sector pay and about half of the average national salary

within_hromada_mismatch.value: 64% of hromadas have at least one preschool understaffed in classroom teachers and another overstaffed

budget_rigidity.value: providers cannot retain or redirect savings across budget lines, so financing rewards prescribed inputs rather than enrollment, quality, or adaptive service delivery

reform_mechanism.value: the 2024 Preschool Law introduces greater flexibility in staffing, service models, governance, and quality assurance, but implementation depends on hromada capacity and practical guidance

observations.method: Expenditure and staffing analysis combined with institutional review, policy analysis, and interviews with national, oblast, hromada, and preschool-institution stakeholders.
observations.uncertainty: The report identifies structural inefficiency and implementation constraints but does not estimate the causal effect of the new law; staffing and budget patterns may change as the law is implemented and as wartime and demographic conditions evolve.
observations.subgroup: Classroom teachers, technical and specialist staff, preschool directors, hromada officials, caregivers, children needing inclusive services, and communities rebuilding or repurposing facilities.
observations.counterinterpretation: Technical and specialist roles may provide valuable care, nutrition, inclusion, and developmental support; reducing them without service-network redesign could worsen quality, workload, or safety.

boundary: This record adds an early-childhood-care-to-territorial-inequality, female-labor-force, and recovery-capacity mechanism. It is a public expenditure and institutional review, not a causal evaluation of wartime disruption, the Preschool Law, household welfare, child development, or labor-market outcomes; the central open test is whether local implementation converts regulatory flexibility and excess capacity into equitable, safe, high-quality access.
